items.title: 16.7 Tests for identification of basic radicals

source_refs.note: Topic 16.7 with Quick Check 16.4, printed pages 345-347. The print labels both iron tests 'f)' and describes the Fe2+ precipitate with ammonia as 'white gelatinous'. The exercise (pages 348-349) is not reproduced.

blocks.text: For each cation (basic radical) about 4 g of the solid sample is dissolved in about 10 cm3 of distilled water and the solution divided into two parts: one part is tested with NaOH solution and the other with aqueous ammonia.

blocks.title: Hydroxide precipitates
blocks.text: Al3+ + 3OH- -> Al(OH)3 white ppt; NH4+ + OH- -> NH3 + H2O; Ca2+ + 2OH- -> Ca(OH)2 white ppt; Cr3+ + 3OH- -> Cr(OH)3 green ppt; Cu2+ + 2OH- -> Cu(OH)2 blue ppt; Fe2+ + 2OH- -> Fe(OH)2 green ppt; Fe3+ + 3OH- -> Fe(OH)3 orange-brown ppt; Zn2+ + 2OH- -> Zn(OH)2 white ppt

The iron(III) test as printed starts from 2 g of FeCl3 rather than an unknown sample. Three cations give white precipitates with NaOH: Ca2+ (insoluble in excess), Zn2+ (soluble in excess) and Al3+ (gelatinous); aqueous ammonia then separates them, since Ca2+ gives almost nothing and the Zn2+ precipitate redissolves in excess. The two iron ions are told apart by colour: Fe2+ gives a green precipitate that browns on standing, Fe3+ an orange-brown precipitate at once.

blocks.caption: Telling similar results apart

Zn(OH)2 dissolves in excess NaOH and in excess NH3; Ca2+ gives only slight turbidity with NH3; Al(OH)3 is gelatinous and insoluble in NH3
Green ppt with NaOH: Cr3+, Fe2+
Cr(OH)3 dissolves in excess NaOH to a green solution; Fe(OH)2 turns orange-brown in air
green turning brown against orange-brown at once
light-blue ppt with NaOH; deep blue solution with excess NH3

blocks.prompt: What is the lake test, how is the ammonium ion indicated, how are Fe2+ and Fe3+ distinguished, and what happens when aqueous ammonia is added to Cu2+ in limited and in excess amounts (Quick Check 16.4; MCQ III, IV; exercise Q.2e, f, g, Q.6)?
blocks.explanation: The lake test confirms Al3+: a little litmus or alizarin solution is added to the suspension of Al(OH)3 and the gelatinous precipitate adsorbs the dye to give a coloured 'lake': Al3+ + 3OH- -> Al(OH)3, then Al(OH)3 + dye -> Al(OH)3.dye (the lake). Ammonium is indicated by warming the sample with NaOH: ammonia with its distinct smell is evolved and turns moist red litmus blue. Fe2+ gives a green precipitate with NaOH that turns orange-brown on standing, while Fe3+ gives an orange-brown precipitate immediately. With a little aqueous ammonia Cu2+ gives a light-blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide; with excess ammonia the precipitate dissolves to a deep blue solution of the tetraamminecopper(II) ion.

items: NaOH: Al3+ white gelatinous; NH4+ ammonia on warming; Ca2+ white (insoluble in excess); Cr3+ green (soluble in excess); Cu2+ light blue; Fe2+ green turning brown; Fe3+ orange-brown; Zn2+ white (soluble in excess).

NH3(aq): Al3+ white; Ca2+ slight turbidity or none; Cr3+ green (insoluble in excess); Cu2+ deep blue solution; Fe2+ precipitate oxidising to red-brown Fe(OH)3; Fe3+ orange-brown; Zn2+ white, dissolving in excess.
